issues.legal_issue: A pre-constitutional central law imposing liability for taxes on Union property does not override the constitutional exemption unless Parliament provides otherwise after the Constitution.
material_facts: The railway property was originally owned by a non-government company and was taxed under a local law and a notification.
After the railway became government-owned, a central law and a later notification provided for payment of local taxes.
The municipality relied on that law to claim taxes on the government-owned railway property.
Parliament had not enacted a post-constitutional law making the Union property liable for the taxes claimed.
issues.conclusion: The pre-constitutional law could not displace the exemption for Union property under Article 285(1); the property was exempt unless the claim qualified under Article 285(2).
issues.legal_principle: Article 285(1) exempts Union property from taxes imposed by a State or an authority within a State unless Parliament provides otherwise by law. Under Article 372(1), existing laws continued only subject to the Constitution. The Railways (Local Authorities Taxation) Act, 1941, was repugnant to Article 285(1) to the extent it imposed taxes on Union property, and was not a post-constitutional law of Parliament providing otherwise.

predicates.municipal_tax_claim_against_union_proper: A local authority claims a tax on property owned by the Union.
predicates.liability_based_only_on_preconstitutiona: The claimed tax liability rests only on a central law made before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.postconstitutional_parliamentary_law: Parliament has enacted a law after the Constitution came into force providing for the claimed tax on Union property.

issues.definition: When a local authority's claim on Union property rests only on a pre-constitutional central law and Parliament has not since provided for the tax, the earlier law does not remove the property's tax exemption.

issues.legal_issue: Changes to the amount of a continuing tax or to the local law under which it is claimed do not, by themselves, make it a different tax for the purpose of the constitutional continuation rule.
material_facts: The municipality had taxed railway property before the Constitution under the municipal law then applicable.
The claim concerned the same kind of municipal taxes on the same railway property after the Constitution.
The amount of tax had varied, and the municipality later relied on a different municipal law after that law was extended to the area.
issues.conclusion: The variation in amounts and the change in the applicable municipal law did not make the tax different from the tax previously levied.
issues.legal_principle: Article 285(2) permits continuation of the tax to which Union property was liable or treated as liable immediately before the Constitution, so long as that tax continues to be levied in the State. The tax remains the same where its nature, type and the property taxed remain the same; variation in amount or a change in the municipal law relied on does not alone alter its identity. The Court relied on Governor-General of India in Council v. Corporation of Calcutta and Union of India through General Manager E.I. Railway v. Municipal Board, Lucknow, and distinguished Town Municipal Committee, Amravati v. Ramchandra Vasudeo Chimote, which concerned Article 277 and new taxes.

predicates.municipal_claim_seeks_continuation_of_ta: A local authority claims to continue a tax that was levied on the property before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.same_kind_of_tax_on_same_property: The nature and type of tax, and the property on which it is levied, remain the same.
predicates.only_amount_or_local_law_changed: The differences relied on are a change in the amount payable or a change in the local law under which the tax is claimed.

issues.definition: A continuing tax remains the same tax when its kind and the property taxed are unchanged, even if its amount or the local law relied on has changed.

issues.legal_issue: A local authority cannot rely on the constitutional continuation rule when it belongs to a different State from the State in which it was located before the Constitution came into force.
material_facts: The municipality was a local authority in one State before the Constitution came into force.
The area administered by the municipality was later transferred to another State.
The municipality claimed to continue levying the pre-constitutional tax on Union property after that transfer.
issues.conclusion: The municipality could not rely on Article 285(2), because it was no longer a local authority in the same State in which it had been located before the Constitution came into force.
issues.legal_principle: Article 285(2) permits a local authority to continue levying a tax on Union property only so long as that tax continues to be levied in “that State.” The Court held that this requires the claiming local authority to be in the same State in which it was before the Constitution came into force.

predicates.municipal_tax_claim_against_union_proper: A local authority claims a tax on property owned by the Union.
predicates.tax_was_levied_before_constitution: The local authority levied the tax on the property before the Constitution came into force.
predicates.authority_now_in_different_state_than_be: The local authority is now in a different State from the State in which it was located before the Constitution came into force.

issues.definition: If a local authority seeks to continue a pre-constitutional tax on Union property after moving into a different State, the continuation exception is unavailable.
